name: Niagara Green
lede: Niagara Green is a pale, greyed blue-green named for Niagara Falls, the waterfalls on the border of Canada and the United States, and recorded as a color standard since 1912.

sections.title: A waterfall's name
sections.body:
Niagara Falls is the collective name for three waterfalls on the Niagara River between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, one of them, Horseshoe Falls, among the highest-flow-rate waterfalls in the world [3]. Ridgway's 1912 standards plate this green on plate XXXIII, hue 41 double-prime, tone b, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary later filed the same swatch, block 163, as a pale green, 5.4 units from that block's center [1]. Our library gives it the Munsell notation 7.1G 7.0/2.6 [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are Dark Bluish Glaucous, 3.3 units away, and Eggshell Green, 3.4 units away [1]. A paler member of the same name, [[pale-niagara-green]], sits in our library too, lighter and less saturated than this one [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Niagara Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in 109 works, under half of one percent [2]. The earliest dated example is Andrea del Castagno's 1450 portrait of a man, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1910s, in 8 of 523 paintings, more than three times the archive's overall rate for that decade, and it turns up in Gustav Klimt's paintings here thirteen times the baseline rate [2]. Eighty-one percent of its appearances sit in a painting's highlights rather than its mid-tones or shadows [2]. It shares a canvas with [[sage]] more than any other color word, over eleven times the baseline [2]. These are screen-color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
